Integrating LLM and Diffusion-Based Agents for Social Simulation

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: ; xxx xx–xx, xxxx; xxx, xxCCS: Applied computing Sociology
Xinyi Li email: lixinyi22@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: DCST, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China , Zhiqiang Guo email: georgeguo.gzq.cn@gmail.com Affiliation: DCST, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China , Qinglang Guo email: gql1993@mail.ustc.edu.cn Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China , Hao Jin email: jinhao1@cetc.com.cn Affiliation: China Academy of Electronics and Information Technology, China , Weizhi Ma email: mawz@tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: AIR, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China and Min Zhang email: z-m@tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: DCST, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
2025
Abstract.

Agent-based social simulation provides a valuable methodology for predicting social information diffusion, yet existing approaches face two primary limitations. Traditional agent models often rely on rigid behavioral rules and lack semantic understanding of textual content, while emerging large language model (LLM)-based agents incur prohibitive computational costs at scale. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid simulation framework that strategically integrates LLM-driven agents with diffusion model-based agents. The framework employs LLM-based agents to simulate a core subset of users with rich semantic reasoning, while a diffusion model handles the remaining population efficiently. Although the two agent types operate on disjoint user groups, both incorporate key factors including user personalization, social influence, and content awareness, and interact through a coordinated simulation process. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods in prediction accuracy, validating the effectiveness of its modular design. The code is available11 1 https://github.com/lixinyi22/Social-Simulation-for-Information-Diffusion.git.

Keywords: 
Social Simulation, Inforamtion Diffusion, Agent-based Model

1. Introduction

With the rapid advancement of information technology, online social media has become deeply integrated into the daily lives of the public, serving as a crucial platform for information generation and diffusion (Yuan et al., 2016). Gaining a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying information diffusion in social networks has become an essential foundation for advancing modern social governance and optimizing the public information environment. Research in this area spans multiple analytical levels, ranging from microscopic models of individual behavior (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016) to macroscopic analyses (Yu et al., 2011; Yuan et al., 2016) of population-level interactions.

Among these approaches, agent-based models (ABMs) offers a simulation framework that captures how local interactions among individual agents generate emergent global diffusion dynamics (Jackson et al., 2017), enabling the study of hypothetical scenarios without real-world consequences. have been widely used to simulate collaborative social behaviors and phenomena and reveal their critical importance. These approach treat each agent as an autonomous individual. Through rule-driven interactions of between agents, simulation process reveals how and why information spreads in some extend, therefore it transcends mere prediction task. Furthermore, it provides a vital platform for conducting "what-if" analyses, such as assessing the impact of intervention policies or platform algorithm changes prior to real-world implementation. However, traditional ABMs also exhibit notable limitations: agent behaviors are typically governed by preset rules, making it difficult to adapt to human decision-making in complex social contexts. Moreover, conventional mathematical models struggle to integrate multi-source heterogeneous information (e.g., text, images), restricting their applicability in large-scale social environments.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a new pathway for building more expressive agent models. LLMs can not only understand rich semantics and multi-modal information, but also simulate human-like value judgments, emotional variations, and behavioral logic, thereby enhancing the realism and responsiveness of agents in social simulations. Currently, LLM-based agents are being deployed in various virtual social scenarios (Mou et al., 2024a). However, these methods also face significant challenges, primarily high computational costs and considerable generation latency. In real-world social media environments with tens of thousands of users and intricate interaction networks, deploying an LLM agent for each user leads to drastic efficiency degradation, hindering practical scalability.

To address the above limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-empowered hybrid simulation agent framework for social information diffusion prediction, aiming to provide an more flexible and low-cost way to simulation information diffusion process while maintaining a high level of accuracy in individual-level behavior. The core design orchestrates a cooperation between LLM-based agents and diffusion model-based agent: a core subset of users is emulated by LLM-driven agents, while the remaining majority are represented by a data-driven diffusion model. By continuously expanding the user groups activated by information within the simulation, the outcomes of the two agent behaviors were flexible integrated. Be more specific, we first select a subset of core users played by LLM-driven agents. By integrating their historical behaviors, profile attributes, and decision-making mechanisms, these agents dynamically respond based on information content. Subsequently, based on the behavioral outputs from these agents, we employ an information diffusion model to infer individual-level user behavior across the entire user set.

Our framework incorporates the three key factors identified in our contributions: user personal interests, inter-user influence and post content in both kind of agents. For the LLM-based agent, these factors are reflected in the user information stored within. And for the the diffusion model-based agent, these factors are reflected in the algorithm used to learn the user history during the training process, as well as the initial input produced by the LLM-based agents. This synergistic integration enables a topic-aware, personalized, and collaborative simulation. To evaluate our framework’s effectiveness, we conduct experiments on real-world diffusion datasets collected from Weibo and Zhihu. Results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms both traditional models and fully agent-based simulation in terms of prediction accuracy.

In summary, the main contributions of our work are as follows:

  1. (1)

    We proposed a hybrid architecture capable of simulation of user behaviors in specific scenarios based on real data empowered by LLM and personalized collaborative filtering. This enables fine-grained individual-level generative modeling for information diffusion prediction.

  2. (2)

    Our simulation framework flexiblely incorporates three key aspects: user personal interests, inter-user influence, and post content characteristics, enhancing the topic-aware, personalized and collaborative simulation process.

  3. (3)

    We conduct extensive evaluation on multiple real-world social media datasets. Experimental results show that our method achieves high simulation accuracy in modeling both individual behaviors prediction and overall diffusion scale.

2. Related Work

2.1. Social Information Diffusion Prediction

The study of information diffusion modeling focuses on understanding how individuals perceive and relay information through social connections (Guo et al., 2024). Modeling information diffusion processes in social networks has long been a foundational research challenge. Early approaches (Wang et al., 2014) often conceptualized diffusion as a sequential process, estimating the probability of information transfer between pairs of users. With advances in deep learning and growing insights from communication theory, a wider variety of methodological principles have been introduced to address this problem spans multiple analytical levels and methodological perspectives. A number of studies (Wu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2019) adopt a microscopic view, constructing fine-grained models of individual user behavior to forecast future actions, while others (Zhong et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2021) emphasize macroscopic patterns by modeling global user interactions. In addition, several works (Turkoglu and Mutlu, 2023) perform large-scale statistical analyses of real-world social media data to uncover attributes of content that are most likely to gain user engagement and propagate widely.

Agent-based modeling (Deffuant et al., 2000; Hegselmann, 2015) represents one established line of inquiry in this domain. This simulation-based approach captures how local interactions among individual agents—each representing a user—can give rise to emergent global diffusion patterns (Chuang and Rogers, 2023). A key strength of such simulations is to model hypothetical scenarios that have not yet occurred in reality, allowing researchers to examine potential outcomes without real-world consequences. As a result, agent-based social simulation serves as a valuable tool for assessing and mitigating the adverse impacts of information spread.

2.2. Traditional Model-driven Agent-based Social Simulation

Traditional model-driven agent-based social simulation has explored a variety of mechanisms to govern agent, including weighted averagin (DeGroot, 1974), Bayesian inference (Madsen et al., 2018), and differential equations (Baumann et al., 2020). Despite their apparent diversity, many of these models share a common underlying structure, built upon components that capture assimilation, reinforcement, and repulsion forces among agents (Chuang and Rogers, 2023). In such frameworks, each agent typically maintains a continuous internal state reflecting certain user attributes, and interactions between agents iteratively update these state values (Chuang and Rogers, 2023). The emergence of deep learning has introduced neural networks with capable of predicting collective user behavior as an alternative form of social simulation. By organizing users in sequential or graph-based structures, these models (Yang et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024c) learn latent representations and forecast which users or items are likely to be engaged next.

However, a fundamental limitation of such methods above lies in their lack of semantic comprehension. Since simulations are conducted through purely numerical processes, they cannot directly interpret linguistic input. Instead, textual content must be converted into embeddings, a step that inevitably introduces information loss and noise.

2.3. Social Simulation with LLMs

The emergence of LLMs has spurred growing interest in their application to social simulation, leveraging their robust language understanding and generative capabilities. Research in this area spans multiple scales, from individual-level to society-level simulation. At the individual level, studies (Xu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023) often employ LLMs to emulate specific personas—such as public figures or occupational roles—with an emphasis on behavioral fidelity. As the scope expands to multi-agent settings, researchers have integrated diverse social contexts, including group debates (Wang et al., 2024a), classroom interactions (Chen et al., 2023), and so on. External elements like recommender systems (Wang et al., 2024b) or online platforms (Zhang et al., 2023) are often incorporated to enhance environmental realism as well.

A major limitation of LLM-driven social simulation is its substantial computational cost. Conducting a full-scale simulation in which each agent invokes an LLM per information item would require millions of API calls when the scale of user and information up to thousand level, rendering such approaches economically prohibitive. Furthermore, although several recent platforms (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025) claim to support simulations involving tens of thousands of agents, these systems often prioritize generative scalability over task-specific optimization and real-world alignment. This trade-off can result in poor performance when evaluated at the level of individual agent behavior.

3. Simulation Framework

3.1. Task Definition

Let 𝒰={u1,u2,…,uM}\mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{M}\} denote the universal set of users in a social network. An item of unpropagated information (e.g., a newly created post) is represented as p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P}, where 𝒫={p1,p2,…,pN}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{N}\} is the set of all such information pieces. Each information pp in 𝒫\mathcal{P} is associated with a tuple of attributes: (content,publisher,publish time)(\text{content},\text{publisher},\text{publish time}).

In our simulation scenario, upon the introduction of a piece of information pkp_{k} into the simulation framework, each agent (representing a user uju_{j}) determines whether to interact with it, such as by reposting or commenting. After the simulated diffusion process concludes for pkp_{k}, we will obtain a diffusion record rk=(u1k,u2k,…,u|rk|k)r_{k}=(u_{1}^{k},u_{2}^{k},\dots,u_{|r_{k}|}^{k}), which is a set of users who were activated by and interacted with the information, where each uik∈𝒰u_{i}^{k}\in\mathcal{U}.

Besides, user history is also provided in our simulation. For each user uju_{j}, their history is defined as hj={(aji,tji)}h_{j}=\{(a_{j}^{i},t_{j}^{i})\}, a set of triples, indicating that user uju_{j} performed a behaviour ajia_{j}^{i} at time tjit_{j}^{i} in response to a specific information item pip_{i}. The collective history of all users is denoted ℋ={h1,h2,…,hM}\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},h_{2},\dots,h_{M}\}.

Given the set of unpropagated information 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the complete user interaction history ℋ\mathcal{H}, the goal of the social information diffusion task is to predict the diffusion record rkr_{k} for each information item pk∈𝒫p_{k}\in\mathcal{P}. That is, to forecast the complete set of users who will be activated by pkp_{k} during the simulation.

3.2. Overall Framework

Figure 1 provides a overview of our proposed hybrid simulation agent framework. The simulation process for a new piece of information pkp_{k} begins with LLM-based agents. Each LLM-agent is initialized with a comprehensive user information, consist of static profile, historical comments and publishment on the social media. Guided by a multi-stage decision framework, each agent evaluates the content of pkp_{k} to generate its decision.

The engagements generated by the LLM-based agents serve as a seed cascade for the diffusion model-based agent, which has been pre-trained on the historical interactions of the entire user set 𝒰\mathcal{U}. This model leverages collaborative signals and user preference patterns to estimate the activation probability for every user in the network. The final predicted cascade is constructed by combining the LLM-agent engagements with the topK most probable users identified by the diffusion model, thereby generating a complete individual-level prediction of the diffusion sequence.

This hybrid design circumvents the prohibitive computational cost of deploying LLM-agents for all users, by cooperating with diffusion model for majoriay. Concurrently, it overcomes the cold-start problem inherent to traditional diffusion models when predicting unpropagated information, by providing them with a semantically rich and simulated seed diffusion result from the LLM-agents.

3.3. LLM-based Agent

To capture the complexity of human decision-making process in social media, we employ LLMs to empower a selected subset of core user agents, due to the advanced capabilities of LLMs in semantic comprehension of the information content and value alignment with the user personal interest, which allow them to generate human-like responses in a context-aware manner.

In our framework, each LLM-based agent represents a specific user provided with user profile and historical interactions. We designed a structured multi-stage decision-making framework tailored to the online social platforms through carefully designed prompt templates that guide the agent to evaluate whether its assigned user would engage with the given piece of information. Since this paradigm is entirely training-free, it enables our simulation to be efficiently and flexibility adapted to diverse scenarios. The detailed prompt templates for each stage are provided in the appendixA.

3.3.1. User Description

The LLM-based agent is completely driven by prompt and is equipped with a comprehensive description constructed from user historical data. We carefully design it with two components: a structured User Profile and a detailed User Historical Interactions Record.

User Profile

The User Profile is designed to provide a multi-faceted representation of the user’s behavior pattern and interests on social media. consist of four attribute: Social connections, personality traits, opinion focus category, and activity level. Specifically, social connections include user’s community affiliations, identified by applying the Louvain algorithm to their historical interaction data. Personality traits is a distillation of the user’s behavioral disposition, summarized into 3-5 descriptive adjectives. Opinion Focus is expressed as a list of topics each associated with a confidence score. Both personality traits and opinion focus category are generated by GPT-4O-Mini based on user historical records. Activity Level is a quantitative measure of the user’s overall engagement intensity on the platform.

User historical interactions

User historical interactions logs two primary types of events: publish behaviours and interactive behaviours. The publish behaviours records containing the full content and timestamp of information published by the user, while records of interactions with existing information (e.g., reposting, commenting) include not only the content and timestamp of the source information but also the content and timestamp of the user’s reactive.

3.3.2. Multi-stage Decision Framework

This framework is designed to guide the agents in evaluating information and simulating human decision-making patterns, comprising two core components: Decision Strategies and Multi-stage Decision-making Process.

Decision Strategies

Decision strategy bases behavioral decisions on the following three principles:

  1. (1)

    Consider edge cases: Even if a post doesn’t perfectly match, consider if it could be interesting.

  2. (2)

    Balance quality and quantity: Aim for meaningful recommendations while avoiding empty results.

  3. (3)

    Use relative scoring: Compare posts within the user’s context rather than absolute standards.

Multi-stage Desicion-making Process

The multi-stage decision-making process consists of three stages to make the entire decision-making process clearer and more controllable.

  1. (1)

    STAGE 1: Initial Assessment. This stage is a quick filter. Posts that are clearly irrelevant or inappropriate are rejected at this stage with a "No" decision.

  2. (2)

    STAGE 2: Comprehensive Evalution. This stage evalute information content in a weighted scoring mechanism applied across four aspects: textitEngagement Potential (25%), Content Alignment (35%), Personalization Factors (25%), and Diversity & Discovery (15%).

  3. (3)

    STAGE 3: Desicion Logic. This stage translates the quantitative score from Stage 2 into a definitive action.

3.4. Diffusion Model-based Agent

Building upon the simulated results generated by the LLM-based agents, the diffusion model-based agent is tasked with predicting subsequent users across the entire network. Diffusion model-based agent leverage collaborative signals latent in user interaction histories, thereby capturing the complex interplay between user-information relationships and user-user influences that underpin personalized interests and social dynamics.

To model user behavior from multiple scale, our diffusion agent employs a dual-encoder architecture to learn user representations. One of them is the global encoder that learns user embeddings from the global interaction graph to model global social influences, and the other is local encoder that learns user embeddings from local, information-specific interaction sequences to capture dynamic, context-dependent behaviors. This multi-scale modeling strategy ensures a comprehensive user representation for accurate diffusion prediction.

3.4.1. Global Scale Learning

This component is designed to learn user representations by capturing cross-cascade patterns from global interaction structures. Drawing inspiration from established research (Yuan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024c; Cheng et al., 2023) in information diffusion, we follow heterogeneous graph-based approaches as the foundation for modeling user global representation.

We construct a heterogeneous graph 𝒢𝒽\mathcal{G_{h}} that integrates two complementary structures derived from all information cascades: a user-user interaction hypergraph 𝒢​u​u\mathcal{G}{uu} and a user-information interaction hypergraph 𝒢​u​i\mathcal{G}{ui}. In 𝒢​u​u\mathcal{G}{uu}, nodes represent individual users, while hyperedges encode group interactions. Specifically, each hyperedge corresponds to a central user AA and connects all user groups that have interacted with AA, thereby modeling higher-order social influences. Conversely, in 𝒢​u​i\mathcal{G}{ui}, nodes represent users while hyperedges represent information items. Users who have interacted with the same information are connected by the corresponding hyperedge, capturing shared interest patterns.

To efficiently extract latent user representations from both 𝒢​u​u\mathcal{G}{uu} and 𝒢​u​i\mathcal{G}{ui}, we employ a Light Hypergraph Neural Network (LHGN). This streamlined architecture omits activation functions and feature transformations to focus on capturing pure structural patterns. The propagation rule for each graph component is defined as:

Xil+1=Dv−1​Hi​De−1​Hi⊤​Xil\textbf{X}_{i}^{l+1}=\textbf{D}_{v}^{-1}\textbf{H}_{i}\textbf{D}_{e}^{-1}\textbf{H}_{i}^{\top}\textbf{X}_{i}^{l}

where X​i0\textbf{X}{i}^{0} denotes the initial user embeddings, D​v\textbf{D}{v} and D​e\textbf{D}{e} represent the node and hyperedge degree matrices respectively, and H​i\textbf{H}{i} is the matrix of each graph component. After LL layers of propagation, we aggregate the multi-scale representations through layer-wise averaging:

Xi=1L+1​∑l=0LXsl\textbf{X}_{i}=\frac{1}{L+1}\sum_{l=0}^{L}\textbf{X}_{s}^{l}

Finally, we integrate the complementary embeddings from both graph components using an attention mechanism that adaptively weights their contributions:

αi=e​x​p​(a⋅Wa​Xi)∑j∈u​u,u​ie​x​p​(a⋅Wa​Xj),X=∑i∈u​u,u​iαi​Xi\alpha_{i}=\frac{exp(\textbf{a}\cdot\textbf{W}_{a}\textbf{X}_{i})}{\sum_{j\in{uu,ui}}exp(\textbf{a}\cdot\textbf{W}_{a}\textbf{X}_{j})},\textbf{X}=\sum_{i\in{uu,ui}}\alpha_{i}\textbf{X}_{i}

where a∈ℝd\textbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and Wa∈ℝd×d\textbf{W}_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are learnable parameters that determine the relative importance of each graph component in the final user global representation.

The model takes as input a sequence of the last n users’ local embeddings 𝐗′i0\mathbf{X^{\prime}}^{0}_{i}. To preserve temporal order, we incorporate a learnable positional encoding matrix 𝐏∈ℝn×d\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} resulting in the input representation 𝐗′^i0=𝐗′o0+𝐏\hat{\mathbf{X^{\prime}}}_{i}^{0}=\mathbf{X^{\prime}}^{0}_{o}+\mathbf{P}.

We then employ a masked multi-head self-attention mechanism to capture dependencies within the sequence:

Attention​(𝐐,𝐊,𝐕)=softmax​(𝐐𝐊⊤d+𝐌)​𝐕\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V})=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}+\mathbf{M}\right)\mathbf{V}

where 𝐌∈{0,1}n×n\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n} is a causal mask matrix that ensures the representation at position can only attends to positions up to previous positions in the sequence. Finally, a feed-forward network processes the attention outputs to generate the local user representations:

3.4.3. Prediction and Fusion Gate

The prediction layer estimates the relevance between the target information and all candidate users to generate a ranked list of potential adopters.

To construct the information representation, we aggregate the embeddings of users who have previously interacted with the it. Specifically, we compute average pooling over the global and local user embeddings separately:

𝐙g=AvgPool​({𝐗i}),𝐙l=AvgPool​({𝐗′i})\mathbf{Z}^{g}=\text{AvgPool}(\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\}),\quad\mathbf{Z}^{l}=\text{AvgPool}(\{\mathbf{X^{\prime}}_{i}\})

We introduce a gated fusion mechanism to dynamically integrate these complementary representations:

γ=s​i​g​m​o​d​(𝐖⁡[LN​(𝐙g);LN​(𝐙l)])\gamma=sigmod(\mathbf{W}[\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}^{g});\text{LN}(\mathbf{Z}^{l})])
𝐙=γ⊙𝐙g+(1−γ)⊙𝐙l\mathbf{Z}=\gamma\odot\mathbf{Z}^{g}+(1-\gamma)\odot\mathbf{Z}^{l}

where LN​(⋅)\text{LN}(\cdot) denotes layer normalization, σ\sigma is the sigmoid function, and 𝐖∈ℝ2​d×d\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d\times d} is a learnable parameter matrix. The fused representation 𝐙∈ℝd\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} undergoes dropout regularization before prediction.

For user representation, we prioritize the local embedding 𝐗′\mathbf{X^{\prime}} as it better captures user-specific interests relevant to individual information items. The activation score for each user is computed via dot product:

y^=𝐙⊤​𝐗′+Mmask\hat{y}=\mathbf{Z}^{\top}\mathbf{X^{\prime}}+M_{\text{mask}}

Here, Mmask∈ℝNM_{\text{mask}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is a binary mask that assigns −∞-\infty to users already activated in the current cascade, preventing duplicate predictions during inference.

The model parameters are optimized using cross-entropy loss:

ℒC​E=−∑i=2|𝒫|∑j=1|𝒰|yi​jlogsoftmax(y^i​j)\mathcal{L}_{CE}=-\sum^{\left|\mathcal{P}\right|}_{i=2}\sum^{\left|\mathcal{U}\right|}_{j=1}y_{ij}\log\text{softmax}(\hat{y}_{ij})

4. Expriments

4.1. Experimental Setup

4.1.1. Datasets

We construct two online social media platform: Weibo and Zhihu to conduct the experiments.

Weibo

The Weibo dataset is built around several trending topics that have spurred public discussion in recent years, capturing diverse user reactions to emerging information. We collected data from Sina Weibo via keyword-based filtering, retaining posts along with their content, publication time, and associated interactions—including comments, reposts, and corresponding user identifiers and timestamps. On Weibo, both commenting and reposting behaviors are treated as user activations. Thus, each original post and the set of users who commented on or reposted it collectively form an information cascade.

Zhihu

The Zhihu dataset (Hao et al., 2021) is collected from a knowledge-sharing platform (Zhihu). It contains the anonymous descriptions of users, answers, questions, authors, and topics, along with approximately 100 million interactions user-question interactions. On Zhihu, answering a question is considered a user activation. Each question and all of its associated answers are treated as one information cascade.

To balance dataset scale with computational feasibility while maintaining a realistic user base size, we sample from both sources. From the Weibo dataset, we select two subsets: one concerning the Israel–Palestine conflict, characterized by high discussion volume, and another on the “3·15” starch adulteration incident, with more moderate activity. The Zhihu data are randomly downsampled. We further apply the following filtering steps: (1) if a user interacts with the same post multiple times, only the earliest interaction is retained; (2) information with fewer than three interactions are discarded to ensure meaningful diffusion paths. Table 1 summarizes the final dataset statistics.

4.1.2. Baseline Methods

We evaluate our simulation framework against four categories of baseline methods, representing distinct methodological paradigms in social simulation:

  1. (1)

    POP: Naive rules-based simulation framework. A rule-based simulation method that recommends the most frequently active users for all information items based on historical interaction counts, serving as a simple yet classic baseline.

  2. (2)

    AgentSociety (Piao et al., 2025): LLm-driven generative agent simulation framework. AgentSociety is a large-scale social simulator powered by LLM-driven agents situated in realistic virtual social environments. It supports modeling rich social behaviors through generative interaction.

  3. (3)

    HiSim (Mou et al., 2024b): Hybrid-driven Agent Simulation Framework. HiSim partitions users into core users modeled via LLMs and ordinary users modeled via deductive agent-based models. Content generated by core users is converted into attitude scores to influence the behavior of ordinary users.

4.1.3. Implementation Details

We partition all datasets into training, validation, and test sets with a ratio of 8:1:1. We evaluate all methods using recall, precision, F1-score, and accuracy computed by comparing the set of ground-truth activated users against the set of users predicted by each simulation framework.

For all LLM-based agent methods, including our framework, AgentSociety, and HiSim, we configure 100 core users per test sample, represented by LLM-driven agents. These users include all ground-truth activated users in the sample, with the remainder randomly sampled from negative users. A very small number of test sample with more than 100 ground-truth users is excluded. All LLM-based agents are implemented using GPT-4o-mini, and only historical interactions from the training set are used to construct agent memory.

In our diffusion model-based agent, we use the Adam optimizer with a batch size of 64, a learning rate of 1e-3, and an embedding size of 64. The model outputs a ranked list of users by confidence score. We extract the top-k users as predictions, where k∈{10,20,50}k\in\{10,20,50\} is chosen based on the average propagation length in each dataset. The POP baseline follows the same top-k selection strategy. The model is trained on GeForce RTX 3090.

In AgentSociety, we initialize each agent memory with its full interaction history. For each test information item, we use the platform’s built-in survey mechanism to collect forwarding or commenting decisions from all agents, treating all responding users as predictions.

In HiSim, ordinary users can only output an attitude score in [−1,1]\left[-1,1\right]. We consider a user activated if their attitude change exceeds 0.5 with a max simulation turns as 6. We use the built-in BCMM model to drive ordinary users, with the bc bound parameter set to 0.9. We init ordinary users’ attitude score with their history record.

4.2. Overall Performance

Table 2 summarizes the overall experimental results. Our framework achieves the highest F1-score and presicion across all datasets, and yields suboptimal yet competitive performance even without best k-value, substantially surpassing all baseline models. Although our method does not exceed HiSim in recall on the Weibo-Sausage and Zhihu datasets, it achieves the second-best results with a marginal gap. More importantly, our method exhibits a more balanced trade-off between recall and precision than HiSim, as reflected in the F1-score. Since most of users are inactive, which is align with the prediction of baselines and our approach, accuracy gets universally high on all dataset.

It should also be noted that the high sparsity of our dataset adversely affects certain baselines, though is consistent with real-world conditions. Since users in HiSim lacking historical records begin with an attitude score of zero and exert minimal influence on others throughout the simulation, regardless of the number of rounds, thereby maintaining unchanged attitudes from start to end. Due to the prohibitive computational cost associated with LLM API calls in AgentSociety, the corresponding results have been excluded from the overall comparison.

We also observe that as k increases, our framework’s recall improves at the expense of precision and F1-score. This indicates that including low-confidence users identified by the diffusion model does not contribute meaningfully to the outcome since most of them are negative users, and overly expanding the candidate set is ineffective.

4.3. Ablation Analysis

4.3.1. LLM-based Agent

Figure 2 presents the results of our ablation study on LLM-based agents, which was conducted on 100 core users under four configurations: providing only user profiles, only user history, complete user description, and both user description and the multi-stage decision framework. For comprehensive comparison, we also include the results of relevant LLM-based baselines.

The ablation results indicate that the LLM-based agent equipped with both the complete user description and the multi-stage decision framework achieves the best performance in most cases, and at least the second-best across all metrics and datasets. This confirms that each component in our design contributes effectively to the overall task.

We further observe that the LLM exhibits a strong capability to autonomously extract useful information from raw input, surpassing setups that rely on manually pre-extracted features. Among the ablated settings, using only user profiles yields the weakest results, whereas incorporating user history leads to significant improvements. Moreover, the integration of structured decision rules consistently enhances performance, suggesting that explicit human-coded rules help guide the LLM in interpreting social scenarios more accurately.

When compared with baseline methods, AgentSociety delivers poor performance, likely because its agents are designed for broader generative tasks rather than being specialized for diffusion prediction. This generality may prevent the agents from accurately identifying relevant attributes and making appropriate decisions within the complex action space. HiSim achieves higher recall but lower precision and F1-score than our method, a trend that aligns with observations from the overall experiments.

4.3.2. Diffusion Model-based Agent

Table 3 presents the results of our ablation study on the diffusion model-based agent, where we evaluate three distinct representation settings: using only user global representations, only user local representations, and a combined representation, under identical simulation outcomes generated by the LLM-based agents.

The results indicate that all three representation schemes achieve competitively high performance across the evaluated metrics. While the performance gaps among them are relatively small, the combined representation method attains the best scores in more scenarios, suggesting a complementary effect between global and local user features in the diffusion modeling process.

4.4. Parameter Sensitivity Analysis

4.4.1. LLM-based Agent Number

Figure 3 illustrates the impact of varying the number of LLM-based agents in the simulation. We evaluate four configurations: no LLM-based agents, where the diffusion model relies solely on the ground-truth propagation data in the first hour after published; and settings with 100, 300, and 500 LLM-based agents. As the number of agents increases, randomly selected negative users are incorporated into the original candidate set of LLM-based users.

The results reveal that employing more LLM-based agents does not consistently improve performance. With an increasing number of such agents, overall prediction performance tends to decline. On Weibo-conflict and Zhihu datasets, both F1-score and accuracy exhibit a clear decreasing trend. Although the Weibo-sausage dataset does not show a strictly monotonic decrease, its performance at 300 and 500 agents is still inferior to that at 100 agents. This degradation occurs because a larger agent pool increases the proportion of users with minimal historical activity, whose behavior is inherently harder to predict, thereby reducing overall simulation quality.

At the same time, the inclusion of LLM-based agents remains essential. The no-agent configuration yields the poorest results across most metrics—except accuracy—even though it uses partial ground-truth information. This is attributed to the cold-start problem, which severely limits the diffusion model’s effectiveness. Since most pieces of information do not propagate sufficiently within the first hour, the diffusion model lacks adequate data to make reliable predictions.

4.4.2. Different LLM Model

Table 4 compares the performance of the LLM-based agent component and the full framework when instantiated with two different base models: GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-80B. The results indicate a substantial performance gap between the two model choices, with Llama-3.1-80B yielding significantly inferior outcomes compared to GPT-4o-mini across most evaluation metrics. This performance disparity can be attributed to reasoning capability, and model’s instruction-following ability, which is essential for generating well-structured and parsable responses from the simulated agents is important as well.

5. Conclusion and Future Work

In this work, we present an integrated simulation agent framework for social information diffusion prediction. The framework combines the complementary strengths of LLM-based agents and traditional diffusion models to balance simulation accuracy with computational efficiency. LLM-based agents first simulate a subset of core users, after which diffusion model-based agents complete the remainder of the simulation, enabling a flexible and interactive coupling of the two simulation paradigms.

Our approach incorporates user personalization, inter-user influence, and content awareness. Based on historical user behavior data, both agents incorporate the behavioral characteristics of all users into their model parameters and can also affect each other. This design also allows the two agent categories to mutually influence one another during the simulation process. Experimental evaluation on three real-world datasets demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods.

For future work, we plan to extend the framework to support additional predictive tasks, such as forecasting the scale of activated users or incorporating temporal dynamics. These extensions would enable a more comprehensive simulation of social information diffusion processes.
